PART B - Basic Data Types: typesof(), class(), and mode()
```{r}
x <- 42
y <- 42L
z <- "42"
w <- TRUE
v <- 3+2i

typeof(x)
typeof(y)
typeof(z)
typeof(w)
typeof(v)
```

```{r}
class(x)
class(y)
class(z)
class(w)
class(v)
```

```{r}
mode(x)
mode(y)
mode(z)
mode(w)
mode(v)
```

PART C - Type Conversion
```{r}
num_string <- "123"
num <- as.numeric(num_string)
typeof(num)
class(num)
mode(num)
```

```{r}
as.logical(0)
as.logical(1)
```

```{r}
bad_string <- "hello123"
num <- as.numeric(bad_string)
```

Question #5
 Why do you think R is designed to give a warning here rather than crashing the whole script?
 - its to allow data processing pipelines to continue running smoothly even when encountering unexpected errors

 What are the risks of this behavior if you don't read your warnings?
 - Because it can lead to the silent propagation of values that will silently corrupt calculations without you knowing

PART D - Strings paste(), and paste0 ()
```{r}
first <- "Juan"
last <- "Dela Cruz"

print(first)
print(last)
```

```{r}
first <- "Juan"
last <- "Dela Cruz"

paste(first, last)
paste0(first, last)
```

```{r}
paste(first, last, sep = "-")
```

```{r}
full_name <- paste0(first, last, sep = "-")
age <- 21
paste0(full_name, "is", age, "years old.")
```

Question #10

CONCLUSION
In R, data types such as logical, integer, double, and character determine how information is stored and handled. During arithmetic, R uses implicit coercion, which often turns logical values into numbers without notice but produces errors when characters are involved. Knowing typeof() and class() is important because they let you check the exact structure of your data before working with it, which helps avoid unexpected behavior. Being comfortable with functions like as.numeric() and as.character() also helps make sure combined data and calculations give predictable, accurate results without breaking your workflow.
